Consider a disk with a block size of $512$ bytes. A block pointer is $8$ bytes long. A data file contains $50,000$ STUDENT records of fixed-size $147$ bytes. In this file, the key field is ID$\#$, whose length is $12$ bytes. The file is unspanned and ordered by the key field ID$\#$, and a primary index is constructed on ID$\#$.

Let $A$ be the total number of first-level index entries and $B$ be the total number of first-level index blocks required for this configuration. Calculate the value of the expression: $3 A+4 B$.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

$\left(3^{*} 16667+4^{*} 695\right)$

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Step 1: Calculate the Number of Blocks for the Data File

Because the file is unspanned, a record cannot be split across two blocks.

  • Number of records per data block:

    $R_{fb} = \lfloor \frac{\text{Block Size}}{\text{Record Size}} \rfloor = \lfloor \frac{512}{147} \rfloor = \lfloor 3.48 \rfloor = 3 \text{ records/block}$

  • Total number of data blocks :

    $N_b = \lceil \frac{\text{Total Records}}{R_{fb}} \rceil = \lceil \frac{50000}{3} \rceil = 16667 \text{ blocks}$

Step 2: Calculate First-Level Index Entries 

A primary index is a sparse index that contains exactly one entry for each block of the data file.

  • Total number of index entries :

    $A = N_b = 16667$

Step 3: Calculate First-Level Index Blocks 

  • Size of an index entry :

    $R_i = \text{Key Size} + \text{Block Pointer Size} = 12 + 8 = 20 \text{ bytes}$

  • Number of index entries per block

    $R_{ib} = \lfloor \frac{\text{Block Size}}{R_i} \rfloor = \lfloor \frac{512}{20} \rfloor = \lfloor 25.6 \rfloor = 25 \text{ entries/block}$

  • Total number of index blocks :

    $B = \lceil \frac{A}{R_{ib}} \rceil = \lceil \frac{16667}{25} \rceil = \lceil 666.68 \rceil = 667 \text{ blocks}$

Step 4: Calculate the Expression Value

now we substitte the values of A = 16667 and B = 667 into the given expression:

3A + 4B = 3(16667) + 4(667)

50001 + 2668 = 52669

Final Answer

52669

Each record has a total size of $123$ bytes (including all data fields and metadata). The data file is physically unspanned and ordered on disk by the primary key field Ssn, whose length is $9$ bytes.

A single-level primary index is constructed on the Ssn field. Each index entry consists of a primary key value and a block pointer. Calculate the total number of blocks required to store this first-level primary index on disk.

  • Total number of data blocks 

    $\lceil \frac{\text{Total Records}}{\text{Records per block}} \rceil = \lceil \frac{30000}{4} \rceil = 7500 \text{ blocks}$

Step 2: Calculate First-Level Index Entries

we will have sparse index containing exactly one index entry for each data file block.

Consider a disk with a block size of $512$ bytes. A block pointer is $6$ bytes long, and a record pointer is $7$ bytes long. A data file contains $30,000$ EMPLOYEE records of fixed size $123$ bytes using an unspanned organization. The data file is not ordered by the key field $Ssn$, which is $9$ bytes long.

A single-level secondary index is constructed on this non-ordering key field $Ssn$. Calculate the number of blocks required to store this secondary index.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Step 1: Determine the Number of Secondary Index Entries

A secondary index constructed on a non-ordering key field must be a dense index. This means it contains exactly one index entry for every single record in the data file.

  • Total number of index entries (n) = 30,000 entries

Step 2: Calculate the Size of an Index Entry

Since the data file is unordered, secondary index entries must point directly to the individual records using record pointers instead of block pointers. Block pointer size  is given to confuse heree.

  • Size of one index entry = Key Size + Record Pointer Size = 9 + 7 = 16 bytes

Step 3: Calculate Index Blocks Required

  • Index entries per block = $floor(Block Size / Index Entry Size)$= $floor(512 / 16)$ = 32 entries/block

  • Total number of index blocks = $ceil(Total Index Entries / Index entries per block)$= ceil(30000 / 32) = ceil(937.5) = 938 blocks

Final Answer: 938

Since Level 3 requires exactly 1 block, it becomes the root of the multilevel index, and make uss stops here.

  • Total blocks = B1 + B2 + B3 = 221 + 7 + 1 = 229 blocks

options.html: Primary index is usually a non-dense index because it is the main index for a table requiring it to be most efficient.
A clustering index is non-dense because the data file is physically ordered on the clustering field, allowing one index entry per distinct value.
Multiple secondary indexes can be created because they are on non-key attributes.
Multi-level indexes can be built on top of any type of first level indexes (primary, secondary and clustered).

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

 

  1. Primary index is a non-dense index because it is the main index for a table requiring it to be most efficient.

    $\textbf{True}$. (It requires that the table be ordered on the indexing attribute)
     
  2. A clustered index is non-dense because sorting is needed to keep the duplicate values together (cluster).

    $\textbf{True}$. Each entry of the clustered index points to the page containing the pivot element (the first value of the cluster (duplicates)). 

    A clustering index is built on a file that is physically ordered on a non-key attribute. Since the ordering attribute is not unique, records with the same value are stored together (they form a cluster).

    The index is typically sparse (non-dense) because:

    There is one index entry for each distinct value of the clustering field (or one per block containing that value), not for every record. Each index entry points to the first block containing records with that clustering value.

    The fact that duplicate values are kept together is a consequence of the file being ordered.

  3. Multiple secondary indexes can be created because they are on non-key attributes.

    $\textbf{False}$. (Secondary indexes do not require the table to be sorted while a table can be sorted only on one attribute. As a result multiple indexes can be created. Secondary indexes are dense indexes)
     
  4. Multi-level indexes can be built on top of any type of first level indexes (primary, secondary and clustered).

    $\textbf{True}$. in multi-level indexing each index level is sorted. Because the three indexes (primary, secondary and clustered) are themselves sorted, multi-level indexing can be built on top of them.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

 

Statement 1: True

  • Reason: A primary index is created on an ordered key field. It only requires one index entry per data block (making it a sparse/non-dense index). This design minimizes the index size, allowing it to fit into main memory for maximum search efficiency.

Statement 2: True

  • Reason: A clustering index is built on a data file physically ordered by a non-key field. Because all identical values are physically grouped together across blocks, the index only needs one entry per distinct value of that field, making it non-dense.

Statement 3: False

  • Reason: Multiple secondary indexes can be created, but the statement says they can only be on non-key attributes. In reality, secondary indexes can be created on both key and non-key attributes as long as they are non-ordering fields.

Statement 4: True

  • Reason: A multi-level index is simply a B-tree or B+ tree structure built on top of a first-level index to reduce index block access time. It can be successfully implemented regardless of whether the first level is primary, secondary, or clustered.

questions.html:
A data file contains $1,000,000$ unspanned tuples stored on a disk with a block size of $4096$ bytes ($4\ K$). The configuration parameters and indexing structures are defined as follows:

  • Each data tuple has a fixed size of $300$ bytes.
     
  • Each search key is $4$ bytes long, and each block/record pointer is $4$ bytes long.
     
  • The data file occupies $76,924$ unspanned disk blocks.
     
  • A single index block can store up to $512$ index entries.
     
  • Based on these layouts, a dense index requires $1,954$ blocks, while a primary sparse index requires $151$ blocks.

Assuming a binary search is utilized wherever an ordered structure or index file is searched, which of the following statements are correct regarding the maximum block accesses required to retrieve a target record? (Select all that apply)

options.html: If the data file is ordered by the search key but lacks any indexing mechanism, searching for a record requires at most $17$ block accesses.
Utilizing a single-level primary dense index requires at most $12$ block accesses to find and retrieve the data record.
Utilizing a single-level primary sparse index requires at most $9$ block accesses to find and retrieve the data record.
Constructing a two-level index structure consisting of a dense first level and a sparse second level requires at most $5$ block accesses to locate and retrieve the data record.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

A. No Indexing Mechanism: so we will do binary search directly on the ordered data file blocks.

  • $\lceil \log_2(76,924) \rceil = \lceil 16.23 \rceil = 17 \text{ accesses}$

B. Single-Level Primary Dense Index so here we will do binary search on the dense index blocks + 1 access to retrieve the actual data block.

  • $\lceil \log_2(1,954) \rceil + 1 = 11 + 1 = 12 \text{ accesses}$

C. Single-Level Primary Sparse Index: we will do biinary search on the sparse index blocks + 1 access to retrieve the actual data block.

  • $\lceil \log_2(151) \rceil + 1 = 8 + 1 = 9 \text{ accesses}$

D. Two-Level Index Structure (Dense First Level + Sparse Second Level)

Let's calculate the exact size and search cost of the second level:

  1. Blocks in Level 1 (Dense): $1,954$ blocks.

  2. Blocks in Level 2 (Sparse): Since one index block stores up to 512 entries, the second level needs:

    $\lceil \frac{1,954}{512} \rceil = 4 \text{ blocks}$

  3. Search Operation: we will do binary search on the 4 blocks of Level 2: $\lceil \log_2(4) \rceil = 2$ accesses.

    • Read the targeted block from Level 1: $1$ access.

    • Read the actual data block from the data file: $1$ access.
      so total 4 access

opt d says atmost 5 access, which is correct .

questions.html:
A database system contains a total of $3,000$ records and uses a secondary indexing architecture with an indirect-bucket scheme to handle duplicate search-key values. The layout parameters of the disk storage system are defined as follows:

  • Each data block can hold a maximum of $3$ data records.
     
  • Each index block can hold a maximum of $10$ key-pointer pairs.
     
  • Each bucket block can hold a maximum of $50$ pure record pointers.

On average, each distinct search-key value appears in exactly $10$ records. In this system, the bucket file is packed continuously back-to-back as a single contiguous sequence of record pointers without any gaps, padding, or wasted space inside the physical bucket blocks (meaning a single bucket block can contain pointers belonging to multiple distinct search keys).
Consider the following figure for understanding:
 



Let $A$ be the total number of physical blocks required to hold the secondary index structure (consisting of both the index blocks and the bucket blocks combined) under this indirect-bucket scheme.

Alternatively, suppose the system does not use a bucket file, and instead uses a dense index where a separate key-pointer pair must be stored in the index file for every individual record in the data file. Let $B$ be the total number of physical index blocks required under this dense index scheme.

Calculate the value of the expression: $A+B$.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Step 1: Calculate $A$ (Indirect-Bucket Scheme Blocks)

The structure consists of two parts: the index blocks and the bucket blocks.

1. Calculate Index Blocks:

  • Total records = 3,000

  • Average records per distinct key = 10

  • Number of distinct search-key values = 3,000 / 10 = 300

  • In an indirect-bucket scheme, the index contains exactly one entry per distinct search-key.

  • Total index entries = 300

  • Entries per index block = 10

  • Number of index blocks = 300 / 10 = 30 blocks

2. Calculate Bucket Blocks:

  • Every record in the database must have a record pointer stored in the bucket file.

  • Total record pointers to store = 3,000

  • Pointers per bucket block = 50

  • Since the bucket file is packed continuously back-to-back without any wasted space or padding:

  • Number of bucket blocks = 3,000 / 50 = 60 blocks

Total Blocks for Scheme A:

  • $A$ = Index blocks + Bucket blocks = 30 + 60 = 90 blocks

Step 2: Calculate $B$ (Dense Index Scheme Blocks)

In a standard dense index scheme without a bucket file, every single record in the data file must have its own separate key-pointer entry in the index file.

  • Total index entries = Total records = 3,000

  • Entries per index block = 10

  • Number of dense index blocks ($B$) = 3,000 / 10 = 300 blocks

So finallyy we get:

  • $A + B$ = 90 + 300 = 390

questions.html:
Consider a secondary index layout utilizing an indirect-bucket scheme under the following constraints:

  • Each data block holds a maximum of $3$ records.
     
  • Each index block holds a maximum of $10$ key-pointer pairs.
     
  • Each bucket block holds a maximum of $50$ record pointers.

The underlying data file contains a total of $3,000$ records. There are no constraints on how records share search-key values. The bucket file is packed continuously as a single contiguous sequence of record pointers without any gaps, padding, or wasted space inside the physical bucket blocks.

Determine the minimum and maximum total number of disk blocks required to store the complete structure (including data blocks, index blocks, and bucket blocks combined).
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Correct Option: c

Step 1: Calculate Constant Blocks (Data File & Bucket File)

The problem states that there are no constraints on how records share search-key values. However, the total number of records remains fixed at 3,000, and the bucket file is packed continuously without wasted space.

  • Data File Blocks: Total records = 3,000. Each data block holds 3 records.

    $$\text{Data Blocks} = \frac{3000}{3} = 1000 \text{ blocks}$$

  • Bucket File Blocks: Every record requires 1 pointer in the bucket file. Total pointers = 3,000. Each bucket block holds 50 pointers.

    $$\text{Bucket Blocks} = \frac{3000}{50} = 60 \text{ blocks}$$

  •  Total:

    $$\text{Data Blocks} + \text{Bucket Blocks} = 1000 + 60 = 1060 \text{ blocks}$$

Step 2: Calculate Minimum Index Blocks

To minimize the index blocks, we must minimize the number of unique search-key values.

  • Scenario: All 3,000 records share the exact same search-key value (1 unique key).

  • Index entries: 1 entry.

  • Index Blocks:

    $$\lceil \frac{1}{10} \rceil = 1 \text{ block}$$

  • Minimum Total Blocks:

    $$1060 + 1 = 1061 \text{ blocks}$$

Step 3: Calculate Maximum Index Blocks

To maximize the index blocks, we must maximize the number of unique search-key values.

  • Scenario: Every record has a unique search-key value (dense distribution of keys).

  • Index entries: 3,000 distinct entries.

  • Index Blocks:

    $$\frac{3000}{10} = 300 \text{ blocks}$$

  • Maximum Total Blocks:

    $$1060 + 300 = 1360 \text{ blocks}$$

Minimum: 1,061 blocks; Maximum: 1,360 blocks
